stances.claim: Disputable presumptions in our statutes and Rules of Court are not new -- but they are 'logical consequences' of facts already proved, not substitutes for the underlying factual findings that secure a conviction beyond reasonable doubt.
stances.rhetorical_move: doctrinal reframe (presumption as consequence, not shortcut)

stances.claim: Unlike Rule 131's disputable presumptions which protect the accused, HB 7814's presumptions damn the accused, inverting the basic protective function of presumptions in criminal procedure.
stances.rhetorical_move: comparison-and-inversion (existing law protects; new bill damns)

stances.claim: The real risk is not the textual presumption but its operational consequence -- overzealous policemen 'taking the role of judges' in determining probable cause for warrantless arrest and search, in an area of law where the Supreme Court itself remains 11-3 divided (People v. Sapla).

Given that no senator has filed a counterpart, the Senate should not 'dive into this dispute' and should instead focus on the pandemic, extreme poverty, and unemployment; if police anti-drug work is the goal, current jurisprudence already suffices.

notable_anecdotes: The 'People of the Philippines v. So-and-so' framing rendered as a numerical asymmetry -- '110 million Filipinos against one lonely accused' -- used as the structural reason the Constitution's presumption of innocence must trump statutory presumptions.

The compressed image of constitutional protection: 'the lowly accused can lean only on the sturdy wall of liberty erected by the Constitution' -- one of CJ's most concentrated metaphors for the Bill of Rights as physical structure.

The judicial-humility argument deployed against police: a divided 11-3 SC in Sapla, after 'sagacious justices have for many decades disagreed,' settled the warrantless-search question only with great difficulty -- yet HB 7814 would invite ordinary policemen to make the same calls on the street.

one_paragraph_summary: Panganiban examines the constitutional objections to House Bill 7814, whose 'disputable presumptions' in drug cases have prompted main sponsor Rep. Robert Ace Barbers into a media overdrive. Barbers argues that disputable or prima facie presumptions are not new -- citing Sec. 5 of the Anti-Fencing Law, Art. 354 of the Revised Penal Code, and the 30+ presumptions in Rule 131 -- but CJ counters that the Constitution itself guarantees a basic right that trumps all of these: the accused 'shall be presumed innocent until the contrary is proved.' Conviction requires proof beyond reasonable doubt drawn from hard facts filtered by strict rules of evidence and due process, not mere presumptions. Presumptions are logical consequences of factual findings, not substitutes for them, and Rule 131's presumptions protect the accused while HB 7814's would damn him. The real risk, CJ argues, is operational: overzealous policemen would 'take the role of judges' in determining probable cause for warrantless arrest and search -- in an area where the Supreme Court itself, in People v. Sapla (June 16, 2020), settled the doctrine only by a divided 11-3 vote after decades of disagreement among sagacious justices. With no Senate counterpart filed, CJ urges the Senate to focus on the pandemic, poverty, and unemployment; existing jurisprudence already arms the police -- what is needed is better training, not redundant law.
